name: ARO-ALK7

lead: ARO-ALK7 is an experimental RNA interference drug directed at ALK7, a receptor involved in fat-cell signalling. Fat-loss followers discuss it as a possible non-appetite route to losing body fat.

RNAi lowers production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene. The chain is less ALK7 signalling, fat cells releasing more stored fat, then fat loss and a leaner look. The only public record is a phase 1/2 first-in-human study that began on 9 May 2025 and plans to enroll 150 adults; no results have been reported.

paras: It is available only in the clinical trial, in adults with obesity with and without type 2 diabetes.
No safety data have been reported. It is investigational and not available by prescription.

angle.text: ARO-ALK7 is an RNAi drug aimed at a fat-cell signalling receptor so fat cells release more stored fat, an appetite-independent route to a leaner look. A single early obesity trial is recruiting.

lead: ARO-ALK7 is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy directed at ALK7, a receptor involved in fat-cell signalling. It is being tested in adults with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, and its relevance to appearance is body fat: if it lowers fat-cell signalling as intended, the outcome of interest is reduced fat mass and a leaner build. It is not approved for any use [1].

The sole clinical information is a trial registration: a Phase 1/2 first-in-human study (NCT06937203) that began on 9 May 2025, is recruiting, and plans to enroll 150 adults [1]. No results have been reported.

On the biology, a 2025 review describes activin E and its adipocyte receptor pathway as regulators of fat-cell lipolysis and diet-induced obesity [2], and a 2026 preprint reports that deleting GDF3, an antagonist of the ActE/ALK7 pathway, reduced adipose lipolysis in obese mice [2].
infobox: Obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes

paras: RNAi drugs lower production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene; here the target is ALK7. Research on the activin E to ALK7 pathway in adipocytes is reviewed in the literature [2], and animal work on the pathway is ongoing [2].

One Phase 1/2 first-in-human trial is registered in adults with obesity with or without type 2 diabetes. It started on 9 May 2025, is recruiting, and has a target enrollment of 150.[1] No results have been identified.

timeline.event: Phase 1/2 first-in-human trial in obesity begins (May).[1]
